bull_thesis: You are being handed a proven, net-cash, double-digit earnings compounder at roughly 7 times forward adjusted earnings because its largest business is in a policy-driven soft patch. Euronet has grown adjusted earnings per share double digits for five straight years (diluted earnings per share $4.41 in 2022 to $6.84 in 2025), through immigration headwinds, currency swings and a hostile 2025 macro, and has reaffirmed a 10-15% growth target for 2026. The balance sheet is a fortress — about $217M of net cash (cash $1.20B against $980M of debt as of mid-2026), so enterprise value is roughly $2.5B against about $671M of trailing EBITDA (earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization), an EV/EBITDA of under 4 times and an EV-to-free-cash-flow of about 9 times. Management returns roughly 85% of earnings via buybacks at a self-calculated 13% locked-in pretax return, shrinking the share count and compounding per-share value. The real engine now is a margin-and-mix shift: owned ATMs (volume-sensitive, ~20% operating margin) are shrinking toward 13-14% of revenue while higher-margin merchant acquiring (~25%+), and issuing/infrastructure (Ren, CoreCard, 40-50% margins) grow — merchant acquiring adjusted EBITDA grew 32% in 2025 and digital accelerators reached 26% of second-quarter-2026 revenue growing 31%. Money Transfer, though pressured, is winning share (its U.S.-Mexico corridor was flat while the market fell ~12%) and its Dandelion network posted record quarters. A sum-of-the-parts on the three roughly-equal segments, plus the net-cash add-back, values the equity comfortably in the $95-119 range. The conditions that must hold: the mix shift keeps compounding faster than owned-ATM and retail-remittance fade, and immigration/remittance pressure proves cyclical rather than structural. (2026-08-10 note: the CoreCard-Unibanca Peru SaaS deal announced August 4 is a small, confirmatory data point for this geographic-expansion leg of the thesis, not a scale-changing one.)
bear_thesis: The cheapness is inseparable from a real question about terminal value. 'Transitory' has now been said for four-plus quarters and just produced a second-quarter-2026 earnings MISS ($2.82 versus $2.97, reported July 30, 2026). The legacy owned-ATM business is in secular decline and its defense (bank-infrastructure contracts) is a promise not yet fully in the numbers. The one financial that is moving the wrong way is cash: trailing free cash flow fell about 33% year over year to ~$282M, so the headline 'double-digit growth' is increasingly manufactured from margin mix and buybacks rather than unit growth — and buybacks flatter return on equity (~30%) while true return on invested capital is only ~10%. What confirms the bear: a second consecutive guide-down, Money-Transfer operating income turning outright negative year over year, or free cash flow failing to recover in the second half.
consensus_delta: Where we disagree with the market: the street still frames Euronet as an ATM-and-remittance operator whose largest business is in structural, not cyclical, decline — hence a Western-Union-style ~7x-earnings tag on a company that just grew adjusted earnings 10% in its WORST recent quarter and has compounded double digits for five straight years. Two street assumptions look wrong. First, that owned ATMs are the business: management has walked analysts through the fact that owned-ATM revenue is already under 20% of the total and heading to 13-14%, with the growth coming from long-term bank-infrastructure contracts that pay 'regardless of how much people spend with cash' — a recurring, switching-cost revenue the market is not multiple-ing. Second, that the remittance weakness impairs terminal value: the U.S.-Mexico corridor was flat while the market fell ~12%, digital transactions grew 35-42%, and Dandelion posted record quarters — Euronet is taking share within a soft market, and management credibly argues its on/off-ramp network is a stablecoin beneficiary, not only a victim. forcing_function: There is no single hard date that forces a re-rating; the forcing mechanism is cumulative and self-driven. valley_of_death: The next 3-9 months carry real, near-term risk that can hit before any re-rate. Second, the cash optics: trailing free cash flow is already down ~33% year over year; management promised money-transfer margin improvement would be 'more back-end loaded,' so if the second half does not deliver the margin recovery, the free-cash-flow narrative weakens further. positioning_washout: No forced, mechanical selling dynamic is in play — this is not a dividend cut or an index deletion that would compel yield or passive holders to liquidate. So the shareholder base is drifting out slowly rather than capitulating in a block — which means the 'wash-out' is a gradual de-rating (the ~10% post-earnings drop toward the 52-week low) rather than a single forced flush. The absence of a mechanical washout slightly weakens the 'buy the panic' framing; the offset is that the price already sits near multi-year-low valuation with a net-cash buyback continuously absorbing supply.

bull_thesis:
Euronet is a payments company where roughly 60% of the profit pool is compounding at more than 30% a year and roughly 40% is shrinking, and the market has applied the shrinking business's valuation to all of it.

The growing part is specific and checkable. Management groups its fastest-growing product lines under one heading and reported on 30 July 2026 that this group grew 31% in the quarter and 35% over the first half, against the 23% plan it had set at its own investor day only three months earlier. That group is now 26% of total revenue. Underneath it are four genuinely good businesses. Merchant acquiring in Greece grew adjusted operating earnings 32% in 2025 and has taken market share from 18% to 24% in three and a half years, with the CrediaBank portfolio adding roughly 10% more merchants and 4,200 more signed organically in the second quarter of 2026 alone. CoreCard, the card-issuing platform bought at the end of 2025, has already displaced an incumbent processor at Unibanca in Peru, which itself processes for nine banks, and signed Upgrade in the United States; management expected no deals for eighteen months and is five or six in. Ria Digital has grown transactions above 30% for four consecutive quarters with more than 90% of volume from repeat customers. And Dandelion, the wholesale payout network, added Mastercard Move plus five other partners in the second quarter and is the kind of asset competitors buy access to rather than build.

The shrinking part is shrinking for reasons that are visible, measurable and at least partly reversing. United States outbound remittance had its first annual decline in more than a decade because immigration enforcement cut the sending population; Brookings data cited by management put net migration near zero or negative for calendar 2025 for the first time in half a century. That is a policy shock to a volume base, not a competitive loss - in the third quarter of 2025 Euronet's United States-to-Mexico corridor was flat while the market fell 12%. Management reported market data showing remittance volume to Mexico growing again over the four months to July 2026, and noted the comparisons get easier from here because the damage began in the second quarter of 2025. Separately, European regulators are requiring banks to maintain cash access, which is turning the cash machine estate from a tourist-volume business into contracted bank infrastructure: bank99 in Austria, UniCredit in Poland and Banco Itau in Paraguay were all signed in the first quarter of 2026, and in Spain the machine count went from 2,000 to 4,000 precisely because banks closed branches and had to outsource.

The valuation is the argument. At $66.45 the shares are about six times what management expects to earn this year on its own measure, against a five-year record of delivering double-digit growth in that measure, most recently 10% in the second quarter of 2026 - the fifth consecutive such quarter. Wall Street's own 2027 estimate is $12.00 a share, which is 5.5 times. Leverage is roughly one to two times operating earnings depending on where in the seasonal cycle you measure, far below Global Payments at 5.6 times or WEX at 4.4 times, and Fitch rates the company investment grade. The convertible bonds that make the reported share count look larger were issued at 0.625% and are far out of the money at this price.

What has to hold: cross-border operating earnings must stop falling by the fourth quarter of 2026; cash conversion must normalise in the second half, so that the reported cash-flow statement starts to look like management's roughly $80-million-a-quarter figure; the payments-infrastructure and epay segments must keep growing mid-single digits to carry the year; and management must hit at least the bottom of its 10-15% earnings growth range, which needs roughly $2.52 in the fourth quarter against $2.39 a year ago.
bear_thesis:
The bear case is not that Euronet is a bad business. It is that the cheapness is measured against an earnings figure the cash-flow statement does not yet support, in a business whose largest segment is in structural rather than cyclical decline, at exactly the moment its funding costs are rising.

Start with cash. Free cash flow for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 was $95 million, against $411 million for calendar 2025 and against roughly $415 million of what management calls adjusted earnings. Reported cash from operations was negative $122 million in the first quarter of 2026 and $26 million in the second, and capital spending in the second quarter nearly doubled year over year to $64.6 million. Management's answer - 'approximately $80 million in the quarter' - is a measure of its own construction that strips out the cash-machine funding swing and cannot be tied back to the audited statements. The seasonal explanation is genuine and probably accounts for most of the gap. But the headline that makes this stock screen cheap, 7.4 times free cash flow, is a 2025 number; the same calculation on the last twelve months is roughly 26 times. If the second half does not restore conversion, the entire valuation case rests on a measure management defines itself.

Second, the quality of the earnings growth. In the second quarter of 2026 adjusted earnings per share rose 10% while reported operating income fell 13.6% and reported net income fell 21%. Management volunteered that excluding two non-cash items 'our operating income would have declined by 9%.' The growth therefore came from below the operating line - from buybacks, and from a share count in the adjusted calculation of roughly 38 million against an audited diluted count of 46.2 million. And the buyback that supplies it has been cut: from $388 million in 2025 to a guided $125-150 million a year, already fully spent in the first half of 2026, with management confirming no additional repurchases are embedded in the outlook.

Third, the structural question. Cross-border payments is 42% of revenue and its operating income fell 35% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. Management attributes this to immigration policy, and the immediate cause is policy. But the shape is structural: a 1% remittance excise tax, a sending population that is shrinking rather than pausing, and a retail storefront channel being disintermediated by digital competitors - including Euronet's own. Western Union, the purest comparison, trades at four times operating earnings and 20% free cash flow yield precisely because the market has decided this is a melting asset. Alongside it, the owned cash-machine estate is guided by management itself from under 20% of revenue down to 13-14%. So roughly 40% of today's profit pool is in managed decline, and the growing 26% is not yet large enough to offset it: consolidated operating margin has slipped from 12.5% in 2025 to 11.6% over the last twelve months, and return on invested capital is about 7.6% and falling - below any plausible cost of capital.

Fourth, the setup. Wall Street models $3.75 for the third quarter against $3.62 a year ago, just 3.6% growth, which means the full-year commitment is now loaded into a fourth quarter that will not be reported until February 2027. The company has missed Wall Street's quarterly number in two of the last three prints, including a $33 million revenue miss in the second quarter of 2026. Management has already reset its growth range once, from 12-16% to 10-15%. A specific promise made to Wolfe Research - 50 to 70 basis points of cross-border margin improvement in 2026 - has now been deferred twice and the segment's margins have gone the other way. Insiders have sold 194,695 shares in the open market against 6,987 bought, roughly 28 sold for every one bought, while arguing publicly that the stock is undervalued.

Finally, financing. Central banks in the United States, Europe and Japan all tightened in the nine days to 18 September 2026 and the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. Euronet carries $2.71 billion of borrowings, funds roughly $1 billion of cash-machine inventory seasonally, has already guided to about $6 million of extra interest expense for the rest of 2026 after refinancing its euro bonds, and has relied on cheap convertible issuance - $1 billion at 0.625% in the third quarter of 2025 - as a structural part of its funding. That window is materially narrower now.

What would confirm the bear case: third-quarter cash from operations on 28 October 2026 that again fails to cover capital spending; any softening of the 10-15% commitment; cross-border operating income down again year over year; or the buyback falling below the $125 million floor.
consensus_delta:
Wall Street is pricing Euronet as a remittance company. It is now, on our numbers, roughly 63% an infrastructure and software company by business value, and that is where the market is wrong.

The first incorrect assumption is that the cross-border segment's decline tells you about the whole. Cross-border payments is 42% of revenue but on our estimates only about 26% of business value, because it carries the lowest margins and deserves the lowest multiple. When its operating income fell 35% in the second quarter of 2026, the shares were marked as though the company were Western Union. They are not: payments infrastructure grew operating income 7% excluding purchase accounting in that same quarter, and epay grew 5%.

The second is the multiple applied to the fastest-growing piece. Card issuing, according to management's own disclosure on the fourth-quarter 2025 call, runs at 40-50% operating margins against just over 20% for the segment as a whole and roughly 25% for merchant acquiring. CoreCard displaced an incumbent processor at Unibanca in Peru within months of closing, and management - who expected no wins for eighteen months - is five or six deals in. The market is valuing that revenue at the blended company multiple of roughly six times. Global Payments and WEX, which are more indebted and growing no faster, get 11 to 12.5 times.

The third is the thinnest part of the argument, and worth naming honestly: the coverage itself has thinned out. Only two price targets were published in the last quarter. The average target over the past year was $98.10; over the last quarter it was $82.00; the single target in the last month was Wolfe Research's $70.00 on 25 August 2026. Analysts are not arguing with this thesis - they have largely stopped arguing at all, which is what creates the gap and also means there is no consensus to be proved wrong on a specific number.

Where we agree with the market and our own prior note did not: the balance sheet is not a fortress. At 30 June 2026 net debt was $1.61 billion, and the free cash flow the cheapness rests on was $95 million over the trailing twelve months. Anyone arguing that this is obviously mispriced has to answer that number first.
forcing_function:
Honestly stated: there is no single event that forces this re-rating, and buying it requires accepting that.

The nearest thing to a dated trigger is the third-quarter report on 28 October 2026, with Wall Street modelling $3.75 a share. It matters not for the earnings number - 3.6% growth is already in the price - but for two lines beneath it: whether cash from operations recovers the way it did in the third quarter of 2025 ($197 million), and whether cross-border operating income stops falling. Those two lines are the entire argument. If both turn, the story changes from 'melting payments asset' to 'infrastructure business with a policy-damaged segment bottoming,' and there is a great deal of room between six times earnings and where the rest of the payments group trades.

The second dated item is somebody else's: Grand Theft Auto VI launches 19 November 2026, and Euronet sells the console credits used to fund it through epay. Management said it immediately saw a positive response to pre-orders but explicitly declined to forecast it, and the date has already slipped twice. Treat it as a possible fourth-quarter tailwind to the segment, not as a reason to own the shares.

The third is slower and, in our view, the one that actually does the work. Management now discloses its fastest-growing product lines as a separate group, which reached 26% of revenue growing 31% in the second quarter of 2026. Simple arithmetic: at that growth rate against a roughly flat remainder, this group crosses about a third of revenue during 2027 and becomes the majority of business value. At some point the market stops applying a Western Union multiple to the whole company. That is a re-rating by accumulation of quarters rather than by event, which is why the sensible horizon is about eighteen months rather than six.

What we are explicitly not relying on: a buyback-driven squeeze, which management has cut from $388 million in 2025 to $125-150 million a year; an activist, of which there is no sign; or interest-rate relief, which the September 2026 central bank decisions have moved firmly in the other direction.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain three specific hazards, and none of them is a solvency event.

First and most important, the cash-conversion test on 28 October 2026. Free cash flow over the twelve months to 30 June 2026 was $95 million - cash from operations of $256 million against capital spending of $161 million - versus $411 million for calendar 2025. Reported cash from operations was negative $122 million in the first quarter of 2026. Management's explanation is seasonal working capital tied to funding cash machines for the summer, and the third quarter is normally when that cash comes back: in 2025 the third quarter produced $197 million of operating cash flow. If it does not this time, the valuation case loses its foundation, because the only remaining support is a non-standard measure the company defines itself.

Second, the guidance path. Management has committed to 10-15% growth in adjusted earnings per share for 2026. The first half delivered $4.40 against $9.70 for all of 2025, and Wall Street models $3.75 for the third quarter - only 3.6% growth. That leaves roughly $2.52 needed in the fourth quarter to reach the bottom of the range and about $3.01, a 26% jump, to reach the top. Management has pre-framed this by telling investors the second and third quarters will represent a smaller share of annual earnings than historically. So the year's credibility now rests on a quarter that will not be reported until February 2027, and the company has missed Wall Street's number in two of the last three prints.

Third, financing cost in a tightening cycle. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September 2026 for the first time since July 2023, voted 12-0, with sixteen of eighteen policymakers signalling another increase; the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan tightened within the same nine days; the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. Euronet carries $2.71 billion of borrowings and funds roughly $1 billion of cash-machine inventory seasonally. Management has already guided to about $6 million of additional interest expense for the rest of 2026 after settling its 700-million-euro bonds in late May. The company has also relied on cheap convertible issuance - $1 billion at 0.625% in the third quarter of 2025 - and that window is now much narrower. None of this threatens the balance sheet at roughly one to two times leverage with an investment-grade rating from Fitch, but every dollar of it comes straight out of earnings per share.

What is not a hazard: there is no maturity wall, no cash burn, and no covenant pressure. This is an earnings grind, not a survival question.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical, forced-selling event here, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than inventing one.

Euronet pays no dividend, so there is no income-fund shareholder base to be flushed by a cut. It is not in a distressed index, faces no lock-up expiry, and has no activist campaign running. The share register is ordinary institutional money; the recent 13F filings that surfaced were small new positions being opened, not liquidations.

What has happened instead is a slow, orderly de-rating - which is often the better setup. The shares are down roughly 24% over twelve months and fell from $73.81 on 4 September to $66.03 on 18 September on no company news at all, while the S&P 500 recovered to 7,772.69 by 21 September. Volume through that decline was unremarkable, around 400,000 to 830,000 shares a day. That is not capitulation; it is disengagement. Coverage has thinned to two published price targets last quarter, from ten over the year. A stock that people have stopped arguing about and quietly stopped owning is exactly the kind that re-rates on a single good print, because there is nobody left to sell.

The one genuine negative in the ownership data is internal, not mechanical: open-market insider activity is three purchases totalling 6,987 shares against eleven sales totalling 194,695 - roughly 28 shares sold for every one bought - by executives who spend their calls arguing the stock deserves a higher multiple. That is not forced selling. It is worse, in a quiet way: it is voluntary selling by the people with the best information.
moderator_conclusion:
Buy now, at moderate conviction - the same call we made on 7 September, at a price 10% lower, with our fair value cut from about $90 to $78 and three errors in our prior note corrected.

What we are buying. Euronet is three businesses, and the market is valuing all three the way it values the worst one. Cross-border payments - Ria, Dandelion, XE - is 42% of revenue and saw operating income fall 35% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 as United States immigration enforcement shrank the population that sends money home. Western Union, the closest comparison, now trades at four times operating earnings and a 20% free cash flow yield because the market has decided that business is melting. Euronet trades at roughly five to six times, which implies the market thinks most of the rest of the company is melting too. It is not. Payments infrastructure grew operating income 7% excluding purchase accounting in that same quarter and contains a Greek merchant-acquiring business that has taken share from 18% to 24% in three and a half years, plus a card-issuing platform running 40-50% margins that has already displaced an incumbent processor at a bank processor serving nine Peruvian banks. epay grew 5%. The product lines management groups as its growth engine are 26% of revenue and grew 35% in the first half, against the 23% plan set at its own investor day three months earlier.

Why the conviction is moderate rather than high, and why we did not raise it despite the cheaper price. Three reasons, all of them corrections to our own prior work. This is not a net-cash balance sheet: net debt at 30 June 2026 was $1.61 billion, a seasonal peak that falls to roughly $570 million at the March low point, but a liability at every date. It does not trade under four times enterprise value to operating earnings; it trades at about 5.4 times on the company's own measure. And the buyback we leaned on has been cut by roughly 60%, from $388 million in 2025 to a guided $125-150 million a year that was already fully spent by 30 June. Separately, the peer group re-rated downward while we were away - Fiserv is down roughly 73% in a year - so the discount we measured in early September no longer exists at that size. Those corrections take back almost exactly what the 10% price fall handed us, which is why the conviction number does not move.

The one thing that would change this call in either direction is free cash flow. Over the twelve months to 30 June 2026 the company converted $256 million of cash from operations and spent $161 million of it on capital, leaving $95 million against a $2.5 billion market value - a fifth of what calendar 2025 produced. Management's answer, roughly $80 million a quarter, is a measure of its own construction that cannot be reconciled to the audited statements, and the seasonal explanation is plausible but unproven. That gap is precisely why this is a moderate-conviction position and not a large one, and it is why the value case holds a four rather than a five. The third-quarter report on 28 October 2026 is where it gets settled.

On the market backdrop. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September for the first time since July 2023, the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan tightened in the same nine days, and the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. We have applied that where it belongs. This thesis does not require rate cuts to work, which is the right posture for this environment - but rising rates are a genuine cost here, not a neutral factor, because the company borrows roughly $1 billion each summer to stock its cash machines and has already guided to about $6 million of extra interest expense for the rest of the year. We have taken that into the numbers rather than assuming it away. We have also given no credit at all to the one dated event on the calendar - Grand Theft Auto VI on 19 November 2026, which drives game-credit sales through epay - because it is a third party's date that has slipped twice and management refused to quantify it. The case stands on the residual value of the business, not on an event.

The shape of the trade. At $66.45, the adverse case is $48 - the price at which the market would be treating the entire company the way it treats Western Union today. The base case is $78, and the favourable case, if the software and acquiring businesses get anything close to the multiples Global Payments and WEX command with two to three times more debt, is $103. There is no floor underneath: no deal price, no tender, no net cash. The 52-week low of $62.50 is a chart level and nothing more, and anyone sizing this position should assume it can be broken.

Size it as a patient position, not a trade. The re-rating here comes from the growing quarter of the business becoming the majority of it, which is an eighteen-month process, not a six-month one.

interrogator_dossier:
# Euronet Worldwide (EEFT) — Forensic Dossier

*Prepared 22 September 2026. Sources: Euronet earnings calls of 24 Apr 2025, 1 Aug 2025, 23 Oct 2025, 12 Feb 2026, 29 Apr 2026 and 30 Jul 2026; company financial statements through the quarter ended 30 June 2026; market data as of 22 September 2026 (share price $66.45, NASDAQ, US dollars).*

Euronet is a global payments company with three businesses: a payments-infrastructure arm built around Europe's largest independent cash-machine network plus merchant acquiring and card-issuing software (revenue of $1.28 billion in 2025, 30% of the total); a digital-content distribution arm called epay that sells gift cards, mobile top-up and game credits ($1.19 billion, 28%); and a cross-border payments arm, Ria money transfer plus the Dandelion payout network and the XE currency business ($1.78 billion, 42%).

---

## 1. Narrative arc

**The story has been re-engineered twice in six quarters, and the second re-engineering is a defensive move dressed as an offensive one.**

In the first quarter of 2025 the framing was pure momentum. Mike Brown, the chairman and chief executive, opened with *"we didn't just tiptoe into double digit growth territory, we kicked in the door"* and the company committed to 12–16% growth in adjusted earnings per share for the year. Management described the business as resting on "two key revenue pillars" — payment and transaction processing, and cross-border foreign exchange. The message was that scale and geographic spread made the company nearly weatherproof.

By the second quarter of 2025 the story expanded through deals: the acquisition of CoreCard, a credit-card processing platform, and a contract to run thousands of cash machines for one of the three largest banks in the United States on Euronet's Ren software. The pitch shifted from "we grow because we are diversified" to "we grow because we are becoming a technology company."

From the third quarter of 2025 the tone turned. Revenue came in *"below our expectations due to softness in certain areas of the business"* across all three segments, and management began leaning on an external explanation — immigration policy, global economic uncertainty — while insisting the problems were *"transitory headwinds, not long-term obstacles."* The fourth quarter of 2025 was described as *"one of the more challenging operating environments that we have faced in some time,"* and the 2026 guidance range was quietly lowered from the 12–16% the company had been delivering to **10–15%**.

The second, larger re-engineering came at the Investor Day in May 2026 and shows up fully in the 30 July 2026 call. Two of the three segments were renamed — "EFT" became "payments infrastructure," "money transfer" became "cross-border payments" — and management introduced a new reporting frame called **digital accelerators**, a cross-segment bundle of the fastest-growing product lines (Ria Digital, card issuing, merchant services, Dandelion). These accelerators are now presented as the lead metric: 26% of revenue, growing 31% in the quarter and 35% year to date against a 23% plan.

This is a meaningful and largely honest disclosure change — the underlying growth is real and verifiable in the segment numbers. But it is also a classic manoeuvre: when the consolidated line stops growing, management re-cuts the business so that the growing 26% is the headline and the shrinking 74% becomes context. Note the language used for the legacy businesses on 30 July 2026: *"these businesses remain highly profitable, cash generative and strategically important, providing the foundation that enables us to invest in higher growth opportunities."* That is how a company describes a funding source, not a growth engine.

**Growth drivers quietly dropped.** In April 2025 management explicitly stopped disclosing cash-machine unit additions: *"we would probably start moving away from that kind of a thing, just so that's just another statistic to have to measure."* By the fourth quarter of 2025 the owned-machine business was reframed as *"slightly less than 20% of our consolidation"* heading to *"13%, 14%, kind of in that ballpark."* Travel-driven machine transactions, the driver management leaned on hardest in 2025, were barely mentioned in July 2026 except as a disappointment.

## 3. Tone and confidence trajectory

**Declining, and unusually legible because the same two executives have spoken every quarter.**

- *April 2025 — offensive.* "Kicked in the door." Reaffirming 12–16%. Dismissing tariffs: *"we do not anticipate any significant direct impact."*
- *August 2025 — offensive, deal-led.* Two acquisitions announced in one call. *"We're a growth business with even more exciting opportunities today than yesterday."*
- *October 2025 — first defensive turn.* Rick Weller, the chief financial officer, opens (rather than the chief executive, a small but real change in running order) and leads with a miss: revenue *"below our expectations."* Mike Brown starts citing the United Nations on global uncertainty. The phrase *"transitory headwinds"* appears.
- *February 2026 — defensive, history-as-argument.* *"One of the more challenging operating environments we have faced in some time."* A full slide devoted to surviving 2008, Indian demonetisation, Greece and Covid. The guidance range is lowered to 10–15%. Mr Weller openly pleads the case for a higher multiple: *"why aren't we getting the same kind of trading multiple?"* Executives arguing with their own share price is a confidence signal, and not a good one.
- *April 2026 — stabilising.* A new head of investor relations, Stephanie Taylor, now runs the call. Adjusted earnings per share +19%. Language tightens around named contract wins.
- *July 2026 — defensive with a new frame.* *"Softer than we expected"* appears twice. **Specificity has improved even as confidence has fallen.** That is the healthiest thing in this file. The July 2026 call quantified the decline in cross-border operating income by cause (60% revenue, 25% marketing investment), named the $3 million of incremental digital marketing, named the $4.7 million of acquisition-related amortisation and the $1.9 million of share-based compensation inflating the segment comparison, and told analysts the interest-expense consequence of settling the €700 million bonds (about $6 million for the rest of the year). Management that were hiding something would not hand over that bridge.

## 4. Guidance credibility

**Score: Medium-High on the annual number; Medium on the quarterly path.**

Euronet has hit its annual adjusted earnings commitment every year of the sequence in this file. The 12–16% range set in early 2025 was delivered (2025 adjusted earnings per share $9.70). The 10–15% range set in February 2026 has been reaffirmed three times without amendment, including on a call where management had to report a revenue miss.

The quarterly record is weaker and is the honest counterweight. Against Wall Street estimates: fourth quarter 2025 **missed** ($2.39 against $2.48); first quarter 2026 **beat** ($1.58 against $1.42); second quarter 2026 **missed** ($2.82 against $2.93) on revenue that came in $33 million light. The screener's beat rate of four out of seven quarters is consistent with this.

**No sandbagging pattern.** If anything, the opposite: Euronet sets a range it can hit and then relies on buybacks and mix to get there when the top line disappoints, which is why adjusted earnings per share can grow 10% in a quarter when operating income falls 9%.

**One promise has been visibly reset rather than missed.** Guidance went from 12–16% to 10–15% between October 2025 and February 2026, framed as a new plan rather than a reduction. And in the first quarter of 2026 Darrin Peller's team at Wolfe Research pressed on a specific commitment — 50 to 70 basis points of margin improvement in cross-border — noting margins were down year over year. Mr Weller's answer was that the benefit would be *"a little bit more back-end loaded."* It was not delivered in the second quarter either; that segment's margins fell further.

## 5. Analyst pressure points

**Where analysts keep pushing and management keeps deflecting:**

1. **Share count.** On 30 July 2026 Josh Levin of Autonomous Research asked directly what share count underpins the 10–15% guidance. The answer — *"another, call it 400,000–500,000 shares less as we go into the rest of the year"* — is a fraction of the question. It does not address the gap between the roughly 38 million shares in the adjusted calculation and the 46 million diluted shares the accounts report once the convertible bonds are counted. That is a 20% difference and nobody has made management reconcile it on a call.

2. **Cross-border and Mexican central-bank data.** Mr Levin also noted that Mexican central-bank data showed *growth* in inbound remittances while Euronet reported a decline. Mr Weller's answer — *"I'd just have to look at your data"* — was a non-answer to the most important disconfirming data point raised all year. This is the question to watch on 28 October 2026.

3. **The buyback.** Vasu Govil of KBW pointed out on 30 July 2026 that the company had already used its full-year buyback range in six months and asked what is embedded in guidance for the back half. Mr Weller: *"We don't have any additional numbers incorporated in the outlook there, really."* Translated: the earnings growth guide does not depend on more buybacks, but it also does not promise them.

4. **A question that later became bad news.** In April 2025 Zachary Gunn of FT Partners asked about regulatory risk to money transfer after United States financial-crime regulators issued geographic targeting orders. Management said *"we don't anticipate any kind of adverse reactions."* Fifteen months later the segment's operating income is down 35% on exactly this axis — immigration enforcement plus a 1% remittance excise tax.

5. **What analysts are not asking.** Nobody has pressed management on why reported cash from operations went negative in the first quarter of 2026, or on the widening gap between free cash flow and adjusted earnings. In a business where working capital swings by hundreds of millions on cash-machine funding, that question should be asked every quarter.

---

## 6. Red flags and green flags

🔴 **Free cash flow is the big one.** Free cash flow for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 was **$95 million**, against $411 million for calendar 2025 and against adjusted earnings of roughly $415 million. Reported operating cash flow was negative $122 million in the first quarter of 2026. Capital spending in the second quarter nearly doubled year over year, to $64.6 million from $34.6 million. Management's own figure — *"approximately $80 million in the quarter"* — is a non-standard measure that excludes the cash-machine funding swing and cannot be tied to the reported statements. The seasonality explanation is real and probably accounts for most of it; but it means the headline "7.4 times free cash flow" that makes this stock screen cheap is a calendar-2025 number, and the same calculation on the trailing twelve months is about 26 times. Anyone buying on the 7.4 must be able to explain why.

🔴 **The convertible-bond share count.** The adjusted earnings per share the company guides on uses roughly 38 million shares; the audited diluted count for the second quarter of 2026 was 46.2 million. The $1 billion convertible issued in the third quarter of 2025 at 0.625% is deeply out of the money at $66, so treating it as debt is defensible — but the two treatments must not be mixed, and the adjusted figure quietly uses the friendlier one.

🔴 **Capital return cut by about 60%** without being framed as a cut (Investor Day, May 2026: $125–150 million a year versus $388 million in 2025).

🔴 **Returns on capital are below the cost of capital and falling.** Return on invested capital is about 7.6% on the trailing twelve months, down from 8.2%. Consolidated operating margin fell from 12.5% in 2025 to 11.6% on the trailing twelve months. This is not a high-return franchise being temporarily depressed; it is a modest-return franchise getting slightly worse.

🔴 **Insider selling.** Open-market activity is three purchases totalling 6,987 shares against eleven sales totalling 194,695 shares — 28 shares sold for every share bought, while management argues publicly that the stock is undervalued.

🔴 **Interest expense is rising into a tightening cycle.** The €700 million bonds were settled in late May 2026 at a higher cost, adding about $1.3 million in the second quarter and a guided $6 million for the rest of the year. The company borrows roughly $1 billion seasonally to stock cash machines. Central banks in the United States, Europe and Japan all tightened in the nine days to 18 September 2026.

🟢 **The digital pivot is producing verifiable, named wins, faster than planned.** Accelerator revenue grew 35% in the first half against a 23% plan. CoreCard displaced an incumbent processor at Unibanca in Peru — a processor serving nine banks — and Mr Brown's account of why is specific and testable: *"Prior to the acquisition, we had an issuing platform, but it was not our leading product… After we announced the acquisition of CoreCard, it changed the narrative of the sales process."* Other named wins: Upgrade, NTT Data, Mastercard Move joining Dandelion, Capcom for direct game-publisher distribution, Uber integrating Ria into its United Kingdom driver app, and exclusive card acquiring across all 4,000-plus dm stores in 14 European countries.

🟢 **Merchant acquiring in Greece is a genuinely excellent business** — adjusted operating earnings up 32% in 2025, market share from 18% to 24% in three and a half years, with the CrediaBank portfolio adding roughly 10% more merchants.

🟢 **Ria Digital has grown transactions above 30% for four consecutive quarters**, with more than 90% of volume from repeat customers — a retention figure that, if accurate, describes a real digital franchise rather than a promotional one.

🟢 **Management is buying shares with cash, not issuing them.** The CoreCard acquisition was structured so that shares repurchased in advance covered the stock issued: *"We essentially have done a cash deal after issuing shares that we just repurchased."*

---

## 7. Hidden signals

**The renaming is the signal.** "EFT" to "payments infrastructure" and "money transfer" to "cross-border payments" are not cosmetic. They move the company's self-description away from two categories the market prices as declining — cash machines and retail remittance — toward two it prices as growing. The businesses underneath did not change on the day of the rename.

**"Diversified" has replaced "growth" as the load-bearing adjective.** In April 2025 diversification was a reason the growth was safe. By July 2026 it is the reason the decline is survivable: *"our geo and channel diversification is enabling us to weather the storm."*

**Management has started pre-explaining seasonality.** On 30 July 2026: *"the second and third quarters are expected to represent a smaller share of annual earnings than they have in historical quarters."* Re-phasing the year in advance lowers the bar for quarters that are about to be weak. It may be an honest consequence of the mix shift toward software revenue. It also conveniently defers the burden of the annual guide to the fourth quarter, which will not be reported until February 2027.

**A new voice with a different register.** Stephanie Taylor took over the calls in April 2026. The 2026 calls open with structured slide walkthroughs and quantified bridges; the 2025 calls opened with Mr Brown's showmanship. The disclosure is better. It is also more managed.

**Capital allocation language has shifted from confident to conditional.** October 2025: buybacks locked in *"a pretax return on investment of approximately 13%."* July 2026: *"we continue to view buybacks as an attractive use of capital… Going forward, we will remain disciplined in capital allocation." "Disciplined"* is what companies say when they intend to spend less.

**A tell about the convertible market.** In August 2025 Mr Weller said the company *"would expect to continue"* using convertible bonds *"with acceptable market conditions and terms."* They then issued $1 billion at 0.625% in the third quarter of 2025 — excellent terms. With the ten-year Treasury now above 5%, that window is a good deal narrower, which matters for a company that has used cheap converts as a structural part of its funding.

---

## 8. Capital-allocation verdict

**Classification: PIVOTING.**

This is not a deteriorating business and it is not a stable one. It is a company deliberately reallocating capital and management attention out of two mature, cash-generative, structurally challenged businesses (owned cash machines, United States retail remittance) into three genuinely better ones (card issuing and processing software, European merchant acquiring, digital cross-border payments). The pivot is real, is producing named competitive wins, and is running ahead of the plan management set at its own Investor Day four months ago. It is also incomplete: the shrinking 74% is still large enough to hold the consolidated numbers down, and will be for at least another four to six quarters.

**The single most important thing to weigh before sizing a position: the free-cash-flow evidence does not yet corroborate the earnings.** Everything attractive about this stock is an earnings story — roughly six times the company's measure of 2026 profit, a five-year record of double-digit growth in that measure, management buying stock. But free cash flow over the last twelve reported months was $95 million on a $2.5 billion market value, and the company's own $80-million-a-quarter figure is a non-standard measure that cannot be reconciled to the reported statements. Either the seasonal explanation holds and cash conversion normalises in the second half — in which case the shares are meaningfully undervalued — or adjusted earnings per share is flattering a business whose cash generation has stepped down, in which case six times profit is not cheap at all. The 28 October 2026 third-quarter report is the first place that gets tested.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and the type matters.** The durable advantages are regulatory-licence and network in character, not brand or pricing power. Euronet holds central-bank authorisations, sponsor-bank relationships and cash-logistics infrastructure in dozens of markets — Mr Brown is right that these *"are a bugger to get into."* Dandelion's payout reach (*"4 billion bank accounts… over 600,000 places"*) is a genuine network asset that a new entrant cannot assemble quickly, and card-issuing platforms carry high switching costs, which is why CoreCard's displacement of an incumbent is notable.

But the evidence does not support calling it wide. Return on invested capital is roughly 7.6% and falling, below any plausible cost of capital; consolidated operating margin has slipped from 12.5% to 11.6%; and the segment carrying 42% of revenue posted a 35% decline in operating income. A wide moat shows up as pricing power in a downturn, and this one did not.

**Moat trend: STABLE, on a split verdict.** The legacy half is eroding and management says so — owned cash machines going from under 20% of revenue to 13–14%, and United States outbound remittance experiencing *"its first annual decline in more than a decade."* The technology half is widening: Greek acquiring share from 18% to 24%, CoreCard winning competitive displacements within months of closing, Mastercard Move joining Dandelion, accelerator revenue compounding above 30%. The consolidated return metric is falling because the shrinking half is still the bigger half. Calling the whole moat "eroding" would mean ignoring the visible share gains; calling it "widening" would mean ignoring the return on capital. Stable is the honest reading, and it is a reading that has to be re-tested every quarter.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL, not terminal.** The structural force is payments disintermediation — cash displacement in the machine network, and the migration of remittance and cross-border value transfer to digital rails, wallets and eventually tokenised settlement. This is a real threat to a meaningful share of today's profit pool. Two things stop it being terminal. First, Euronet owns the disruptor in its own most-threatened category: Ria Digital is growing above 30% and Dandelion is a wholesale payout network that competitors buy rather than build. Mr Weller's framing is self-serving but factually strong: *"You can throw some code together to do a blockchain transaction pretty quickly. But you can't throw together a network that's got 4 billion bank accounts connected to it."* Second, the cash-machine business is being converted from tourist-volume exposure into contracted bank infrastructure, with European regulators actively requiring banks to maintain cash access — a regulatory tailwind that partly offsets the volume decline.

**Is the cheapness a fear-print or a shrinking base?** Predominantly a fear-print, with a genuine shrinking component that has to be underwritten rather than waved away. Roughly 40% of the profit pool — United States retail remittance and owned cash machines — faces real structural decline and deserves a low multiple. The other 60% is growing at 30%-plus and does not. The market is applying the melting-asset multiple to the whole company. That is the mispricing. The risk is that the melting half melts faster than the growing half compounds, and the free-cash-flow line is where that would show up first.

Start with cash. Free cash flow for the twelve months to 30 June 2026 was $95 million, against $411 million for calendar 2025 and against roughly $415 million of what management calls adjusted earnings. Reported cash from operations was negative $122 million in the first quarter of 2026 and $26 million in the second, and capital spending in the second quarter nearly doubled year over year to $64.6 million. The seasonal explanation is genuine and probably accounts for most of the gap. But the headline that makes this stock screen cheap, 7.4 times free cash flow, is a 2025 number; the same calculation on the last twelve months is roughly 26 times. If the second half does not restore conversion, the entire valuation case rests on a measure management defines itself.

Second, the quality of the earnings growth. In the second quarter of 2026 adjusted earnings per share rose 10% while reported operating income fell 13.6% and reported net income fell 21%. Management volunteered that excluding two non-cash items 'our operating income would have declined by 9%.' And the buyback that supplies it has been cut: from $388 million in 2025 to a guided $125-150 million a year, already fully spent in the first half of 2026, with management confirming no additional repurchases are embedded in the outlook.

Third, the structural question. Cross-border payments is 42% of revenue and its operating income fell 35% year over year in the second quarter of 2026. Management attributes this to immigration policy, and the immediate cause is policy. But the shape is structural: a 1% remittance excise tax, a sending population that is shrinking rather than pausing, and a retail storefront channel being disintermediated by digital competitors - including Euronet's own. Western Union, the purest comparison, trades at four times operating earnings and 20% free cash flow yield precisely because the market has decided this is a melting asset. Alongside it, the owned cash-machine estate is guided by management itself from under 20% of revenue down to 13-14%. So roughly 40% of today's profit pool is in managed decline, and the growing 26% is not yet large enough to offset it: consolidated operating margin has slipped from 12.5% in 2025 to 11.6% over the last twelve months, and return on invested capital is about 7.6% and falling - below any plausible cost of capital.

Fourth, the setup. Wall Street models $3.75 for the third quarter against $3.62 a year ago, just 3.6% growth, which means the full-year commitment is now loaded into a fourth quarter that will not be reported until February 2027. The company has missed Wall Street's quarterly number in two of the last three prints, including a $33 million revenue miss in the second quarter of 2026. Management has already reset its growth range once, from 12-16% to 10-15%. A specific promise made to Wolfe Research - 50 to 70 basis points of cross-border margin improvement in 2026 - has now been deferred twice and the segment's margins have gone the other way. Insiders have sold 194,695 shares in the open market against 6,987 bought, roughly 28 sold for every one bought, while arguing publicly that the stock is undervalued.

Finally, financing. Central banks in the United States, Europe and Japan all tightened in the nine days to 18 September 2026 and the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. Euronet carries $2.71 billion of borrowings, funds roughly $1 billion of cash-machine inventory seasonally, has already guided to about $6 million of extra interest expense for the rest of 2026 after refinancing its euro bonds, and has relied on cheap convertible issuance - $1 billion at 0.625% in the third quarter of 2025 - as a structural part of its funding. That window is materially narrower now.

What would confirm the bear case: third-quarter cash from operations on 28 October 2026 that again fails to cover capital spending; any softening of the 10-15% commitment; cross-border operating income down again year over year; or the buyback falling below the $125 million floor.

Treat it as a possible fourth-quarter tailwind to the segment, not as a reason to own the shares.

The third is slower and, in our view, the one that actually does the work. Management now discloses its fastest-growing product lines as a separate group, which reached 26% of revenue growing 31% in the second quarter of 2026. Simple arithmetic: at that growth rate against a roughly flat remainder, this group crosses about a third of revenue during 2027 and becomes the majority of business value. At some point the market stops applying a Western Union multiple to the whole company. That is a re-rating by accumulation of quarters rather than by event, which is why the sensible horizon is about eighteen months rather than six.

What we are explicitly not relying on: a buyback-driven squeeze, which management has cut from $388 million in 2025 to $125-150 million a year; an activist, of which there is no sign; or interest-rate relief, which the September 2026 central bank decisions have moved firmly in the other direction.
valley_of_death:
The next three to nine months contain three specific hazards, and none of them is a solvency event.

First and most important, the cash-conversion test on 28 October 2026. Free cash flow over the twelve months to 30 June 2026 was $95 million - cash from operations of $256 million against capital spending of $161 million - versus $411 million for calendar 2025. Reported cash from operations was negative $122 million in the first quarter of 2026. Management's explanation is seasonal working capital tied to funding cash machines for the summer, and the third quarter is normally when that cash comes back: in 2025 the third quarter produced $197 million of operating cash flow. If it does not this time, the valuation case loses its foundation, because the only remaining support is a non-standard measure the company defines itself.

Second, the guidance path. Management has committed to 10-15% growth in adjusted earnings per share for 2026. The first half delivered $4.40 against $9.70 for all of 2025, and Wall Street models $3.75 for the third quarter - only 3.6% growth. That leaves roughly $2.52 needed in the fourth quarter to reach the bottom of the range and about $3.01, a 26% jump, to reach the top. Management has pre-framed this by telling investors the second and third quarters will represent a smaller share of annual earnings than historically. So the year's credibility now rests on a quarter that will not be reported until February 2027, and the company has missed Wall Street's number in two of the last three prints.

Third, financing cost in a tightening cycle. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September 2026 for the first time since July 2023, voted 12-0, with sixteen of eighteen policymakers signalling another increase; the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan tightened within the same nine days; the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. Euronet carries $2.71 billion of borrowings and funds roughly $1 billion of cash-machine inventory seasonally. Management has already guided to about $6 million of additional interest expense for the rest of 2026 after settling its 700-million-euro bonds in late May. The company has also relied on cheap convertible issuance - $1 billion at 0.625% in the third quarter of 2025 - and that window is now much narrower. None of this threatens the balance sheet at roughly one to two times leverage with an investment-grade rating from Fitch, but every dollar of it comes straight out of earnings per share.

What is not a hazard: there is no maturity wall, no cash burn, and no covenant pressure. This is an earnings grind, not a survival question.
positioning_washout:
There is no mechanical, forced-selling event here, and it is worth saying so plainly rather than inventing one.

Euronet pays no dividend, so there is no income-fund shareholder base to be flushed by a cut. It is not in a distressed index, faces no lock-up expiry, and has no activist campaign running. The share register is ordinary institutional money; the recent 13F filings that surfaced were small new positions being opened, not liquidations.

What has happened instead is a slow, orderly de-rating - which is often the better setup. The shares are down roughly 24% over twelve months and fell from $73.81 on 4 September to $66.03 on 18 September on no company news at all, while the S&P 500 recovered to 7,772.69 by 21 September. Volume through that decline was unremarkable, around 400,000 to 830,000 shares a day. That is not capitulation; it is disengagement. Coverage has thinned to two published price targets last quarter, from ten over the year. A stock that people have stopped arguing about and quietly stopped owning is exactly the kind that re-rates on a single good print, because there is nobody left to sell.

The one genuine negative in the ownership data is internal, not mechanical: open-market insider activity is three purchases totalling 6,987 shares against eleven sales totalling 194,695 - roughly 28 shares sold for every one bought - by executives who spend their calls arguing the stock deserves a higher multiple. That is not forced selling. It is worse, in a quiet way: it is voluntary selling by the people with the best information.
moderator_conclusion:
Buy now, at moderate conviction - the same call we made on 7 September, at a price 10% lower, with our fair value cut from about $90 to $78 and three errors in our prior note corrected.

What we are buying. Euronet is three businesses, and the market is valuing all three the way it values the worst one. Cross-border payments - Ria, Dandelion, XE - is 42% of revenue and saw operating income fall 35% year over year in the second quarter of 2026 as United States immigration enforcement shrank the population that sends money home. Western Union, the closest comparison, now trades at four times operating earnings and a 20% free cash flow yield because the market has decided that business is melting. Euronet trades at roughly five to six times, which implies the market thinks most of the rest of the company is melting too. It is not. Payments infrastructure grew operating income 7% excluding purchase accounting in that same quarter and contains a Greek merchant-acquiring business that has taken share from 18% to 24% in three and a half years, plus a card-issuing platform running 40-50% margins that has already displaced an incumbent processor at a bank processor serving nine Peruvian banks. epay grew 5%. The product lines management groups as its growth engine are 26% of revenue and grew 35% in the first half, against the 23% plan set at its own investor day three months earlier.

Why the conviction is moderate rather than high, and why we did not raise it despite the cheaper price. Three reasons, all of them corrections to our own prior work. This is not a net-cash balance sheet: net debt at 30 June 2026 was $1.61 billion, a seasonal peak that falls to roughly $570 million at the March low point, but a liability at every date. It does not trade under four times enterprise value to operating earnings; it trades at about 5.4 times on the company's own measure. And the buyback we leaned on has been cut by roughly 60%, from $388 million in 2025 to a guided $125-150 million a year that was already fully spent by 30 June. Separately, the peer group re-rated downward while we were away - Fiserv is down roughly 73% in a year - so the discount we measured in early September no longer exists at that size. Those corrections take back almost exactly what the 10% price fall handed us, which is why the conviction number does not move.

The one thing that would change this call in either direction is free cash flow. Over the twelve months to 30 June 2026 the company converted $256 million of cash from operations and spent $161 million of it on capital, leaving $95 million against a $2.5 billion market value - a fifth of what calendar 2025 produced. Management's answer, roughly $80 million a quarter, is a measure of its own construction that cannot be reconciled to the audited statements, and the seasonal explanation is plausible but unproven. That gap is precisely why this is a moderate-conviction position and not a large one, and it is why the value case holds a four rather than a five. The third-quarter report on 28 October 2026 is where it gets settled.

On the market backdrop. The Federal Reserve raised rates on 16 September for the first time since July 2023, the European Central Bank and Bank of Japan tightened in the same nine days, and the ten-year Treasury closed at or above 5% for the first time since 2007. We have applied that where it belongs. This thesis does not require rate cuts to work, which is the right posture for this environment - but rising rates are a genuine cost here, not a neutral factor, because the company borrows roughly $1 billion each summer to stock its cash machines and has already guided to about $6 million of extra interest expense for the rest of the year. We have taken that into the numbers rather than assuming it away. We have also given no credit at all to the one dated event on the calendar - Grand Theft Auto VI on 19 November 2026, which drives game-credit sales through epay - because it is a third party's date that has slipped twice and management refused to quantify it. The case stands on the residual value of the business, not on an event.

The shape of the trade. At $66.45, the adverse case is $48 - the price at which the market would be treating the entire company the way it treats Western Union today. The base case is $78, and the favourable case, if the software and acquiring businesses get anything close to the multiples Global Payments and WEX command with two to three times more debt, is $103. There is no floor underneath: no deal price, no tender, no net cash. The 52-week low of $62.50 is a chart level and nothing more, and anyone sizing this position should assume it can be broken.

Size it as a patient position, not a trade. The re-rating here comes from the growing quarter of the business becoming the majority of it, which is an eighteen-month process, not a six-month one.
